blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: In human perception, pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous stimulus.We find a similar phenomenon in modern self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs): on white noise, which contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few directions of their features still form spatially coherent patterns across the patches, imposed by the features themselves.We call this behavior pareidolia, and the span of these directions the pareidolic subspace.On natural images, it holds most of the feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO.This excess explains why DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features, fall far behind DINO in object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own.Our experiments further show that scaling down their pareidolic subspaces steadily restores their ability to discover objects, so their object emergence is hindered rather than lost.These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: Pareidolia Subspace Calibration(PSC) measures the pareidolic subspace only on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to 31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and 59.9~$\mathcal{J}$ on video object segmentation.To identify the cause of pareidolia, we trace it block by block and find that it forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss; controlled training confirms that an image-level loss alone lets it fade.

Pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a
random or ambiguous stimulus [ 75 ] , like the jack-o’-lantern face that
people perceive in an image of the Sun ( a).
In human perception, pareidolia arises when learned expectations dominate weak or
ambiguous input [ 34 , 31 ] , and it is studied with pure
noise, where the input offers no evidence at all: observers shown pure noise report
faces and letters [ 34 ] , and averaging the noise images that
triggered their reports recovers the internal representation behind them, which
psychophysics models as a template that the observer matches against the
input [ 20 , 38 ] .

blocks.en:
This excess matters for object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised
ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own [ 10 ] .
Object emergence is revealed by grouping patches according to the cosine
similarity of their final-layer keys, the very features in which we find
pareidolia, and it is tested by three standard tasks: unsupervised object
discovery [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] , saliency
detection [ 65 , 52 ] and video object
segmentation [ 66 ] .
When the pareidolic subspace holds most of the variance, it dominates these
similarities, so patches are grouped by the pareidolic pattern rather than by the
objects they belong to.
Accordingly, DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features and large gains on
dense tasks solved by trained heads, fall far behind DINO in object emergence
across diverse tasks ( Fig. 4 ).

To examine how the pareidolic subspace affects object emergence, we rescale it in
DINOv2 and DINOv3: scaling it down steadily restores their object discovery, and
scaling it up degrades it further ( Fig. 4 ).
Object emergence in DINOv2 and DINOv3 is therefore hindered by pareidolia rather
than lost.
These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: since the pareidolic
subspace is a property of the model and appears without any image content, its
directions and their excess variance can be estimated from the
response to noise alone.
We propose P areidolic S ubspace C alibration (PSC), which measures the pareidolic subspace only on a
noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its
directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions, without training
or labels.
Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to
31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and
59.9 𝒥 \mathcal{J} on video object segmentation.

blocks.en:
To further investigate what makes a model pareidolic, we trace its pareidolia index block
by block, which measures how much of the noise response recurs across noise images.
The trace reveals that all the ViTs we examine are strongly pareidolic in their
early and middle blocks.
In the last blocks, DINO becomes far less pareidolic, whereas the models that add a
patch-level loss to its recipe remain strongly pareidolic.
Controlled training confirms that the loss decides: trained from scratch with the
same data, architecture and schedule, a ViT remains strongly pareidolic to its last
block under iBOT’s patch-level loss but becomes far less pareidolic under DINO’s
image-level loss alone, and removing the patch-level loss from a trained iBOT has
the same effect.
This matches how pareidolia arises in human perception, where what is perceived
combines expectations with sensory evidence and pareidolia appears when the
expectations outweigh weak evidence [ 13 , 31 ] .
A patch-level loss rewards such expectations: from the visible context, the model
must predict the features of masked patches whose content its input does not
contain, so it learns strong expectations about patch content, which then surface
even on noise.
DINO’s image-level loss acts only on the [CLS] token, asking the outputs for
different crops of the same image to agree, so the patch features receive no target
of their own and are never trained to fill in content that is absent.

blocks.en:
In summary, our contributions are as follows. • We identify and characterize pareidolia in modern self-supervised ViTs: on
white noise, the leading directions of their features form a spatially coherent
template, faint in DINO and strong in DINOv2 and DINOv3. • We show that the pareidolic subspace of DINOv2 and DINOv3 holds most of the
feature variance on natural images and hinders object emergence rather than
destroying it. • We propose P areidolic S ubspace C alibration (PSC), a simple yet effective training-free
calibration that scales down the pareidolic directions, measured on a single noise
input, and recovers object emergence across diverse tasks. • We trace pareidolia to the training objective: it forms in the middle blocks
under both losses but stays strong to the last block only under a patch-level
loss.

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Human pareidolia arises when learned expectations dominate weak or ambiguous
input [ 34 , 31 ] , in line with accounts of hallucination as
the work of overly strong priors [ 13 ] ; it engages
face-selective cortex [ 22 , 34 , 67 ] , and
macaques share it [ 55 ] .
It is studied with pure noise: observers led to expect faces or letters report them
on about a third of pure-noise images [ 34 , 46 ] , averaging the noise
that observers respond to recovers the internal representation behind their
reports [ 1 , 20 ] , an estimate of the template against which
they match the input [ 38 ] , and a clinical noise
pareidolia test measures the tendency in patients [ 35 ] .
In machine vision, recent work tests whether networks share human face pareidolia
on photographs of illusory faces [ 24 , 21 , 11 ] ,
and white-noise classification images reveal the class templates of
classifiers [ 8 ] .
The pareidolia we find is of another kind: a template of the model’s own that the
dense features of self-supervised ViTs impose even on pure noise, which hinders
their object emergence and can be calibrated without training.

blocks.en: 3 White Noise Reveals Pareidolia
blocks.zh: 3 白噪声启示录

blocks.en:
In studies of human perception, pure noise reveals pareidolia because it offers no
evidence, so whatever pattern is reported comes from the observer.
We run the same test on frozen ViTs and ask whether their features impose a
template when the input has none.
We study three model families, DINO [ 10 ] ,
DINOv2 [ 40 ] and DINOv3 [ 53 ] , with eight models
in total: DINO ViT-S/16 and B/16, DINOv2 ViT-S/14, B/14 and L/14, and DINOv3
ViT-S/16, B/16 and L/16.
For the analyses on natural images in Secs. 3 , 4 and 7 ,
we use the first 500 images of VOC07 trainval.
We find pareidolia in other self-supervised ViTs as well, such as
iBOT [ 74 ] , MAE [ 25 ] and
I-JEPA [ 4 ] . 1 1 1 Supplementary Appendix G measures it
in 24 models from 11 families.

blocks.en: 5 Pareidolic Subspace Calibration

blocks.en:
The findings of Secs. 3 and 4 naturally lead to a training-free
calibration.
Because the pareidolic subspace is a property of the model, a single noise input
reveals its directions together with the excess variance they carry over the
remaining directions.
On natural images, this excess lets the subspace dominate the similarities between
patches, and scaling the subspace down brings the objects back.
We therefore propose P areidolic S ubspace C alibration (PSC), which measures the pareidolic subspace only
on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its
directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.

We take DINOv3-B’s template, its noise response within the pareidolic subspace,

This transfer is possible because the template is a property of the model rather

The probe finds the template through its spatial coherence, but on natural images
it competes through its share of the variance.

shuffled across patches, which keeps its directions and its share but removes its
spatial pattern.

From scratch ( Fig. 8 a), the model with the patch-level loss becomes

From the released iBOT-S ( Fig. 8 c), removing the patch-level loss

blocks.en:
The patch-level loss keeps pareidolia strong to the last block; image-level
training does not prevent it from forming but lets it weaken.
This matches how pareidolia arises in human perception, where what is perceived
combines expectations with sensory evidence and pareidolia appears when the
expectations outweigh weak or ambiguous evidence [ 34 , 31 ] ;
overly strong expectations can even produce a percept with no input at
all [ 13 ] .
A patch-level loss rewards strong expectations: each masked patch must be predicted
from its visible context, with no evidence of its own, so the patch features learn
what a patch is expected to contain, and white noise, which offers no evidence
anywhere, exposes these expectations as a template.
DINO’s image-level loss acts only on the [CLS] token, asking the outputs for
different crops of the same image to agree, so the patch features receive no target
of their own and are never rewarded for such expectations. 9 9 9 More details on
the template are given in supplementary Appendix I .

blocks.en: 8 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8 结论

blocks.en:
The features of modern self-supervised ViTs are pareidolic: on white noise, which
contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few of their directions form a
spatially coherent template.
In DINOv2 and DINOv3, the pareidolic subspace these directions span holds most of
the feature variance on natural images, and their object emergence is hindered by
it rather than lost.
PSC measures this subspace only on a noise input, scales its directions down
without training, and recovers object emergence across diverse tasks.
Pareidolia forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but
stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss.

blocks.en: Appendix D Additional Results on Comparison with Existing Paradigms
blocks.zh: 附录D 与现有范例比较的结果

blocks.en:
Registers [ 14 ] remove the high-norm artifact tokens of DINOv2,
which resemble the attention sinks and massive activations of language
models [ 68 , 54 ] , and test-time
registers [ 27 ] move them into an extra token without retraining.
SINDER [ 62 ] traces such artifacts to singular defects of the network
and repairs them by fine-tuning.
DVT [ 72 ] learns a denoiser for position-dependent artifacts in
the output features and notes that “the fundamental underlying reason behind this
property remains unclear”; RASA [ 58 ] removes the
directions along which a linear regressor predicts each patch’s 2D position; and
Pawlowsky et al. [ 42 ] show that ALiBi positional encoding
reduces positional bias in ViTs.
Each of these works targets a component named in advance, artifact tokens or
positional information, and Object-DINO [ 45 ] aggregates the
object information spread over the queries, keys and values of many heads and
layers.
We instead probe the features with an input that has no content, so that whatever
structure they impose shows without being named.
Registers act on a few tokens, while the pareidolic subspace spans a few dense
directions; and whether a linear regressor can predict position is unchanged by
any invertible map of the features [ 26 , 18 ] ,
whereas the similarities that training-free methods compare are not.
We add two controls: natural-image PCA removes as many leading principal directions
of natural-image keys as PSC calibrates, and global ZCA whitening whitens all
directions of the keys.

blocks.en:
Beyond the DINO lineage, we measure the pareidolia index of the final keys for 24
self-supervised ViTs from 11 families ( Tab. F ) and find the same
pattern as in DINO, DINOv2 and DINOv3: models trained with a patch-level loss are
strongly pareidolic, with κ \kappa from 0.48 to 0.96, whereas models trained with an
image-level loss alone are far less pareidolic, with κ \kappa from 0.08 to 0.24.
The two ranges do not overlap. Figure A follows κ \kappa through the blocks.
Up to the middle blocks, the two groups follow the same trend: the mean κ \kappa of
each group rises over the early blocks, the two means reach the same level, about
0.72, by a relative depth of 0.33, and they stay within 0.03 of each other up to 0.42.
The trends diverge only in the later blocks, where the mean of the models trained
with an image-level loss alone falls steadily, to 0.18 at the last block, whereas the
mean of the models trained with a patch-level loss stays between 0.68 and 0.75.
Pareidolia thus forms under either loss, and only a patch-level loss keeps it strong
to the last block, as in the four families of Fig. 7 .

We ask whether the pareidolic subspace sits in every attention head of the last
block or in a few.
For each head, we measure how much of the subspace’s key energy it holds, pick the
head that holds the least, a choice that needs no labels, and run object discovery
on that head’s keys alone, against the raw full keys and the full keys after
calibration.

对于每一个头,我们测量 亚空间的关键能量有多少 它持有,选择
一个不需要标签的选择,并运行对象的发现
仅凭头部的钥匙, 与生的全键和后部的全键相对
校对.

blocks.en:
The two families differ ( Fig. E a).
In DINOv3-B the heads split: five heads hold 68–85% subspace in their keys and
seven hold 36–46%, so half of the heads carry 82% of the subspace’s key energy.
In DINOv2-B every head holds 44–66%, and half of the heads carry 67%.
The split decides what a single head can do ( Fig. E b).
In DINOv3 the cleanest head alone matches the calibrated full keys for all three
sizes (65.8, 71.5 and 59.0 against 65.5, 67.8 and 59.0 CorLoc on held-out VOC07
images) and raises the raw full keys by 21–33 points.
In DINOv2 the cleanest head is no better than the raw full keys (20.2 and 46.2
against 42.8 and 46.8) and falls 20–45 points short of calibration, because no
head is clean.
